strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: personalization for new federated clients without labeled adaptation data. Combining a shared feature-based gate, selective expert transmission, and anchor-driven specialization is a plausible practical contribution.

The reported results are promising within the evaluated settings: 95.7% accuracy on CIFAR10 and 78.6% on CIFAR100, increasing to 83.27% on CIFAR100 with pretrained expert initialization. The latter substantially exceeds the reported pretrained-model and FedAvg baselines.

Ablations examine pretrained-model quality, expert initialization, anchor sampling, and label heterogeneity. The observed routing collapse and sensitivity to anchor participation provide useful empirical insights, and these limitations are acknowledged.
The system diagram, explicit losses, pseudocode, and basic optimization settings make the main algorithm understandable.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons are substantially confounded by client sampling. Table 1 applies the anchor-heavy sampling policy to the baselines, while Figure 7 shows that this policy can severely degrade FedAvg. On CIFAR10, the reported 93% common expert falls to 58.4% after FedAvg training; Fed-ZERO's 95.7% is only 2.7 percentage points above that available common expert. Baselines need appropriate sampling and tuning before the large claimed advantage can be attributed confidently to the proposed method.

The anchor construction strongly favors the intended specialization. Appendix B explicitly assigns disjoint label blocks covering the label space to anchors, whereas the main text describes selecting diverse clients from an initially partitioned population. The paper does not adequately demonstrate discovering suitable anchors in an existing federation or coping with their limited availability. Evaluation uses only two CIFAR datasets and five or ten test clients; the additional heterogeneity experiment does not fully specify the overlapping-anchor construction.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the data and training procedure used to obtain common-expert checkpoints, the feature extraction layer and router dimensions, exact client sizes and partition procedures, and test-set resampling. No implementation or checkpoint link is provided. Run counts and the meaning of shaded plot bands are unspecified, so variability across initialization and client partitions cannot be assessed.

Selective transmission credibly reduces expert traffic relative to transmitting every expert, but broader efficiency and scalability claims lack measurements. There are no accuracy-versus-bytes, runtime, FLOP, or memory comparisons accounting for the common model and expert storage. Restricting FedMix to two experts matches a communication constraint, but additional controls are needed to distinguish routing benefits from the larger total model capacity available to Fed-ZERO.

The relationship to prior personalized and clustered federated learning is insufficiently developed. FedMix is acknowledged, but the comparisons largely comprise FedMix, FedAvg, and a simple ensemble. Relevant mixture-based approaches such as FedEM and simple feature-based clustering or fixed-routing controls would help establish what the learned gate and anchor mechanism add beyond existing specialization ideas.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Table 5 claims 100% routing accuracy, whereas Appendix C presents Table 4 as routing evaluation with average errors of 27.1% on CIFAR100 and 5.5% on CIFAR10; routing correctness is not clearly defined. The assertion of preserving privacy also goes beyond keeping raw data local: expert selections and model updates are communicated, but no threat model or privacy analysis is supplied. These claims require clarification or narrowing.
